claims.text: A physics-informed machine-learning surrogate integrating in-situ TEM/EDS descriptors will accurately predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure characterized by multilevel chemical fluctuations.
High-resolution TEM/EDS images can provide quantitative descriptors such as fluctuation amplitude and spatial correlation length.
The proposed model will incorporate imaging-derived microstructural descriptors as mediators for mechanical-property prediction.
Controlled and standardized TEM imaging conditions are needed to capture hierarchical microstructural features reliably.
Fluctuation amplitude, interfacial spacing, and correlation length represent the alloy’s multiscale chemical heterogeneity.
Using experimentally measured descriptors allows the surrogate to bypass extensive CALPHAD and first-principles simulations.
The imaging-derived descriptors capture critical stress-concentration and crack-initiation sites.
Chemical heterogeneity descriptors can mediate mapping from hierarchical structure to continuum-scale elastic, strength, and fracture properties.
The surrogate will reduce computational demand by an order of magnitude.
Prediction errors for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness will be approximately 10–15% lower than those of high-fidelity simulation methods.
Current approaches rely on coupled phase-field, CALPHAD, and atomistic simulations and are computationally intensive.
Current approaches have limited accuracy in predicting fracture toughness.
The method becomes unreliable when TEM/EDS electron-beam and imaging conditions are insufficiently controlled.
The method becomes unreliable when the selected descriptors omit important features of the hierarchical heterogeneity.
The method becomes unreliable when mechanically induced microstructural evolution lies outside the training domain.
Prior related studies support a role for compositional fluctuations in mechanical behavior.
Prior related studies support a role for microstructural fluctuations specifically in fracture behavior.
A prospective blinded HfNbTiVAl10 specimen set will be used to compare predictions with measured tensile and mode-I fracture properties.
The hypothesis will be falsified if predictions for the blinded specimens fall outside a ±15% error margin relative to experiment.
